notes: "They found only a few small places." is vague; consider "They found only a few small pieces of land."
"So all the people lived in it." Readers met only Servadac, Ben Zoof, the ship's men and a girl; consider "So everyone went to live in it."
"Servadac went there over the ice." could read more naturally as "Servadac went across the ice to the island."
"But most of the world was gone!" is a little stronger than the other levels (which say most of the land around them was gone); acceptable from the characters' view.
'count' (Russian count) may need a gloss for A2, but context makes it clear he is an important man with a ship.
No conditionals or passive found; 'When Gallia passes close...' is a time clause, not a conditional.
Faithful additions (thin air, water boiling fast, English garrison on the rock, Rosette's dislike of his former pupil) match the novel well.
"so that it numbered about thirty souls" - the colony count in the novel is somewhat lower before Rosette joins; 'a few dozen souls' or simply dropping the number would be safer.
"senseless and still" is literary for 'unconscious'; fine at C1 and not graphic.

summary: All five levels retell Verne's novel faithfully (the night of collision, westward sunrise and six-hour days, lightness, the Russian count's ship, Nina, the English garrison, the mysterious 'Gallia' notes, wintering in the volcano, Rosette found by sail-sled, the balloon return on 1 January) with no film elements. Grammar fits each level, quizzes have single defensible keyed answers, and content is 4+ safe; only minor wording notes remain.
